scenes.title: Discrete vs Continuous Compounding Architecture
scenes.concept: Compare compounding formulas side-by-side and highlight why derivatives require continuous compounding.

beatOutlines.textOutline: Discrete compounding formula A = P * (1 + R_m / m)^(mT)

beatOutlines.textOutline: Continuous compounding formula A = P * e^(R_c * T)

scenes.title: Bond Pricing via Individual Zero Rates
scenes.concept: Formulate bond valuation as a sum of zero-coupon payouts discounted at maturity-matched zero rates.

beatOutlines.textOutline: A bond is a portfolio of individual zero-coupon cash flows

beatOutlines.textOutline: Bond price formula: P = sum(C_i * e^(-r_i * t_i)) + M * e^(-r_n * t_n)
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Discounting each coupon at its dedicated zero rate guarantees no arbitrage

summarySteps: 1. Benchmark Hierarchy: Treasury yields carry tax conveniences; OIS represents true risk-free funding.
2. Compounding Effect: Higher compounding frequencies yield greater exponential terminal wealth.
3. Equivalence Formula: R_c = m * ln(1 + R_m / m) bridges discrete bank quotes and continuous models.
4. Zero Rate Purity: Zero-coupon spot rates eliminate coupon reinvestment risk across maturities.
5. Bond Pricing Reality: Bonds must be priced as portfolios of zero-coupon cash flows at dedicated rates.
6. Par Yield Wedge: In upward-sloping yield curves, the zero curve lies strictly above the par curve.
7. Bootstrap Power: Money market instruments and coupon bonds sequentially unlock zero rates.
8. Systemic OIS Transition: Collateralized derivatives strictly require OIS discounting to remove bank credit risk.
bottomTakeaway: Every cash flow requires its dedicated zero rate; continuous compounding and OIS discounting form the bedrock of derivatives valuation.
